old_observations.text: 4.2 What thoughts are: Inner speech. 21 of the rows (H0559, *ʾāmar*, "to say") are places where the Hebrew says "he *said*" and the ESV renders it "he thought," as in 1 Samuel 18:11: "Saul thought, 'I will pin David…'" The Greek *dialogismos* (G1261) and *logismos* (G3053) are also built on *logos*, "word" [lexical]. In these texts, to think is to speak inwardly. *Caveat:* how many rows show this depends on the ESV's choices.; Devising or planning. H4284 *maḥăšāvāh* (from H2803 *ḥāšav*, "to devise"). These thoughts are designs with a direction. They can be just (Proverbs 12:5), evil (Isaiah 59:7), or God's own plan (Micah 4:12). Because they point somewhere, they can be judged, and they can be abandoned (Isaiah 55:7).; Likening, or interpreting. H1819 *dāmāh* ("to resemble") is used in Psalm 50:21: "you thought that I was one like yourself." Many rows record thoughts that were wrong: Genesis 38:15, Mark 6:49, Luke 24:37, Matthew 20:10, Acts 12:9, Judges 3:24 and 2 Kings 5:11. So a thought is a reading of reality, not reality itself.; Something that grows and matures. 1 Corinthians 13:11: "I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways."; Transient, yet weighty. existing_observations.text: A thought is said within oneself and given as quoted speech in twenty-eight verses: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Saul, David, Naaman, Hezekiah and others each think something and the verse gives it. The code behind most is the verb 'to say', whose lexicon sense includes saying in one's heart; in several the thought is spoken to another in a dialogue.

4.2 What thoughts are: Inner speech. 21 of the rows (H0559, *ʾāmar*, "to say") are places where the Hebrew says "he *said*" and the ESV renders it "he thought," as in 1 Samuel 18:11: "Saul thought, 'I will pin David…'" The Greek *dialogismos* (G1261) and *logismos* (G3053) are also built on *logos*, "word" [lexical]. In these texts, to think is to speak inwardly. *Caveat:* how many rows show this depends on the ESV's choices.; Devising or planning. H4284 *maḥăšāvāh* (from H2803 *ḥāšav*, "to devise"). These thoughts are designs with a direction. They can be just (Proverbs 12:5), evil (Isaiah 59:7), or God's own plan (Micah 4:12). Because they point somewhere, they can be judged, and they can be abandoned (Isaiah 55:7).; Likening, or interpreting. H1819 *dāmāh* ("to resemble") is used in Psalm 50:21: "you thought that I was one like yourself." Many rows record thoughts that were wrong: Genesis 38:15, Mark 6:49, Luke 24:37, Matthew 20:10, Acts 12:9, Judges 3:24 and 2 Kings 5:11. So a thought is a reading of reality, not reality itself.; Something that grows and matures. 1 Corinthians 13:11: "I thought like a child … I gave up childish ways."; Transient, yet weighty. Human thoughts are "but a breath" (Psalm 94:11) and "futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20). Yet God weighs them (Proverbs 15:26), and before the flood they were the measure of human wickedness (Genesis 6:5). God's thoughts, by contrast, are "very deep" (Psalm 92:5), "vast" (Psalm 139:17) and "higher" (Isaiah 55:8–9).

Knowing meets the thoughts in sixteen verses. In thirteen the thoughts are the object of a verb of knowing or perceiving, within four words before the member where the position is stored (Job 21:27, Psa 94:11, Psa 139:2, Psa 139:23, Dan 2:30, Mic 4:12, Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, Luk 11:17, 1Cor 2:11, 1Cor 3:20); in Dan 2:29 it is 7 after, and in Mat 22:16 and Mar 12:14 'opinion' stands 14 and 9 words after 'know'. The knower is the Lord, Jesus or the Spirit in most.

Evil and wickedness meet the thoughts in fourteen verses, within five words in each. Within one word: Pro 15:26, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Jam 2:4; within three: Gen 6:5, Job 21:27, Psa 10:4, Psa 56:5; at four or five: Pro 12:5, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7, Jer 4:14, Eze 38:10, Mat 9:4. In Pro 12:5 the thoughts of the righteous are set beside the counsels of the wicked.

A heart or mind is named with the thoughts in all fifteen verses of the pairing: within three words in Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Dan 2:30, Luk 1:51, Eze 38:10, Mat 15:19, Luk 2:35 and Heb 4:12, and 4 to 9 away in Psa 139:23, Mar 7:21, Jer 4:14, Mat 9:4, Luk 5:22 and Dan 7:28; in Rom 2:15 the conscience stands 3 words before. The thoughts are placed in the heart, mind or conscience of the person.

A heart, mind or conscience is named with the thoughts in all fifteen verses. It is within three words in Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Dan 2:30, Luk 1:51, Eze 38:10, Mat 15:19 (3 before), Luk 2:35 and Heb 4:12, and 4 to 9 away in Psa 139:23, Mar 7:21, Jer 4:14, Mat 9:4, Luk 5:22 and Dan 7:28; in Rom 2:15 the conscience is 3 before. The thoughts are placed in the heart or mind, one of the relations found across the subgroups.

Giving stands with the supposition in twelve verses. Within three words after the member in Jdg 15:2 (3), 1Sa 18:21 (1) and Luk 12:51 (3), giving is the act the thought issues in or the peace supposed to be given; elsewhere it is 4 to 15 words away (Deu 15:9, 1Sa 18:17, Jer 3:19, Jer 40:5, Dan 7:25, Luk 8:18, Joh 13:29, Rom 12:3, 1Cor 13:11).

Knowing and the supposition meet in thirteen verses with different ties. In 1Cor 8:2 (1 to 8 words after) and Ecc 9:10 (1 after) knowledge is what the person thinks he has or what is absent; in Mat 9:4 and Eze 11:5 the thinking is known by another; elsewhere the knowing is 3 to 15 words away in separate clauses (Exo 2:14, Rut 4:4, 2Ki 7:12, 1Ch 28:9, Act 12:9, Rom 1:21, Rom 14:14, 2Cor 10:5).

What is conceived is a son in Jdg 13:5, 13:7, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23 and Luk 1:31, children in Num 5:28, the speaker in Psa 51:5, a people in Num 11:12, trouble, chaff and mischief in Job 15:35, Isa 33:11 and Isa 59:4, and the worst against the speaker in Psa 41:7. The conceiving of a child is the commoner object across the verses.

God is the one who discerns, knows or understands thoughts in Ps 139:2 ('you discern my thoughts'), Ps 94:11 and 1Cor 3:20 ('knows the thoughts'), Isa 66:18 ('I know their works and their thoughts') and 1Chr 28:9, where the Lord 'searches all hearts' and 'understands every plan and thought'. In Ps 139:23 God is asked to know the speaker's thoughts. Jesus is the one who perceives or knows their thoughts in Luke 5:22, 6:8 and 11:17 and in Matt 9:4 and 12:25. In Heb 4:12 the word of God discerns 'the thoughts and intentions' of the heart.

The thoughts are of iniquity in Isa 59:7, of evil in Gen 6:5, against the speaker in Psa 56:5, the words 'there is no God' in Psa 10:4, the wicked's in Pro 15:26 and the righteous's in Pro 12:5 (just), toward us in Psa 40:5 and of the Lord in Mic 4:12; the opinion in Mat 22:16 and Mar 12:14 is of persons and what they appear to be. The object or content of the thought is named in the verse or set beside the word within three words.

Believing, honor, reward and the commandment stand with the thought in Pro 14:15 (the simple believes, 3 words before), Rom 12:3 (faith, 6 after), Jam 1:26 (religion, 12 after), 2Sa 10:3 and 1Ch 19:3 (honoring, 4 after), 1Cor 12:23 (honor, 3 after), Heb 10:29 (punishment, 1 before), Mat 22:17 (pay, 2 after) and Num 36:6 and 1Cor 14:37 (the Lord's command). In each the thought is about something owed, believed or commanded.

Another knows, perceives or discerns the thoughts: Job knows his friends' thoughts (Job 21:27), the Lord knows the thoughts of man (Psa 94:11), you discern my thoughts (Psa 139:2), Jesus knows or perceives theirs (Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, Luk 11:17), the Lord knows what the wise think and finds it futile (1Cor 3:20), the Spirit knows a person's (1Cor 2:11) and the word of God discerns them (Heb 4:12). The verb of knowing stands within four words before the member in most of the verses where its position is stored.

In the verses of the quoted thought the partner collections hold words that are not words of their collection's meaning: the surface 'surely' stands as a member of 'hear' in Exo 2:14, Jdg 3:24, 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 20:26 and 2Ki 5:11; 'unworthy' as a member of 'reward' in Deu 15:9; 'presence' and 'present' as members of 'offer' in Rut 4:4 and 1Cor 7:26; and 'will' as a member of 'desire' in 2Sa 14:17 and 2Ki 7:12. These are recorded as open item #2536 and are not resolved here.

A thought is held as a purpose or plan in Num 33:56, 1Sa 18:25, 2Sa 21:16, 2Ch 13:8, 2Ch 32:1, Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, Rut 4:4 and Phili 1:17: the Lord's purpose, Saul's snare, a giant's killing, withstanding a kingdom, conquering cities, destroying nations, making the people forget, changing the times, telling a kinsman and afflicting Paul. The verb is the same as for a supposition, and the verse gives the purpose within two words of it in several.

The supposition is forbidden, denied or withheld in twelve verses: do not think (Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Joh 5:45), we ought not to think (Act 17:29), that person must not suppose (Jam 1:7), let no one think me foolish (2Cor 11:16), let not my lord suppose (2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33), not to think too highly (Rom 12:3, twice), do not think to yourself (Est 4:13), the heart does not so think (Isa 10:7) and no thought of her future (Lam 1:9). In each the negator reaches the member itself, one to seven words from it.

Small words stand in the units of the surfaces of this group and do not carry the sense of supposing: the connective G1161 in 1Cor 8:2, Rom 2:3 and 2Pe 1:13, G2532 in Rom 1:21, the particles and pronouns H3588A (Gen 20:11), H1931 (Pro 21:29), H0834A (Eze 20:32), H0853 (Neh 6:9), the preposition H0413 (Jer 40:4), the copula H1961 (Deu 15:9) and the returning H7725G (Mic 2:8). They are read in their verses as standalone and were read at stage 1 for what they do.

Evil and iniquitous thoughts are held or planned in Gen 6:5, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7, Jer 4:14 and Psa 10:4, with 'evil' or 'wicked' within five words of the member in each. The thoughts are of the wicked and the verses name the thought and the evil together.

Doing and serving stand with the supposition in twelve verses. 'Do' is the partner in nine verses (ten words, two of them in Num 33:56): Num 33:56 (1 after, 3 before), Luk 12:17 (4 after), Gen 18:29 and 18:30 (6 and 9 after), Rom 2:3, 1Cor 7:36, Eze 18:14, Ecc 9:10, Eph 3:20; 'serve' is 12 words before in 1Ch 28:9, 'service' is 2 words after in Joh 16:2 and 'minister' 16 after in Phili 2:25. In Num 33:56 and Luk 12:17 the doing is what is purposed or asked within four words of the thought.

The Lord's own thoughts are stated as done and known by those who hear: his thoughts toward us are multiplied (Psa 40:5), very deep (Psa 92:5), precious (Psa 139:17), higher than ours (Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9) and not known by the nations (Mic 4:12, plan 4 words after). The Lord's thoughts are named beside his works in Psa 92:5 and Isa 66:18.

Fear and the supposition meet in six verses. In Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, 2Sa 14:15 and Neh 6:9 the fear stands 1 to 2 words before the thought and the thought arises from it; in Luk 24:37 the startled and frightened are 3 and 1 words before; in Gen 20:11 the fear of God is 3 words after, as what the thought says is absent. Fear precedes the supposition in five of the six.

Death words and the supposition meet in seven verses. In Gen 26:9, Job 29:18 and Jon 1:6 the dying or perishing is 2 words after the member and is the content of the thought; in Joh 11:13 death is 3 words before and the disciples suppose something else; in Act 8:20 perishing is 4 before, in 1Cor 4:9 death is 7 after and in 1Sa 20:3 it is 15 after. What is feared or foreseen as death is the commonest matter supposed.

Two kinds of partner meet the supposition. The word 'surely' (flagged in #2536 as not a word of hearing) stands 1 to 5 words after the member in five Hebrew verses, inside the quoted thought; hearing proper stands 2 words after in Mat 6:7 (they think they will be heard), 12 before in Luk 8:18 and 7 after in 2Cor 12:6. Only Mat 6:7 ties hearing to the supposition.

Conceiving is foreseen as an announcement in Jdg 13:3, 13:5 and 13:7, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23 and Luk 1:31 (you shall conceive and bear a son), made by the angel of the Lord, by the Lord or by an angel to a woman, and as a condition in Num 5:28 (a clean woman shall conceive). The act stands in the future and is paired with bearing a son in each of the announcements.

War, return and the endurance of a held position stand with the thought in 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 (war, 5 after), 1Sa 18:17 (fight and battles), Mic 2:8 (war, 1 after), Jer 3:7 (return, 5 after, expected and not done), Heb 11:15 (return, 8 after, what thinking of the land would have allowed), 2Ch 13:8 (withstand, 1 after) and 1Cor 7:26 (remain, 9 after). The thought is of conflict, of return or of holding out.

In these verses the act is a refusal as the grammar states it: Jesus rules out the supposition that he came to abolish the Law or bring peace, accuse you, or that God is like an image; Paul rules out thinking too highly of oneself and asks that no one think him foolish. The refusal is of a supposition about Jesus, about God or about oneself, and is spoken by Jesus, by Paul and by the one counselling.

Sin, judging and evil stand with the supposition in Luk 13:2 (worse sinners), Eze 18:14 (a son who sees his father's sins), Rom 2:3 (you who judge), Joh 5:45 (accuse), Mat 9:4 (evil, 1 word after), Psa 64:5 (evil, 5 before), 1Cor 14:20 (evil, 2 before) and Pro 21:29 (the wicked, 5 before). In Mat 9:4 the evil is what is thought; in the others it stands in the clause of the person who thinks.

A view is asked of the hearer in eight verses, where Jesus or the writer puts the question and the hearer's opinion is what is sought: what do you think, Simon (Mat 17:25), a man with a hundred sheep (Mat 18:12), a man with two sons (Mat 21:28), is it lawful (Mat 22:17), what of the Christ (Mat 22:42), which of the three (Luk 10:36), the feast (Joh 11:56) and how much worse a punishment (Heb 10:29). The direction of the asking runs from the speaker to the hearer.

*dialogizomai / dialogismos* | Honest troubled reasoning · hardened anxious reasoning · inner questioning seen by Jesus · reasoning together into murder · self-talk of the rich man · quarrel, dispute, opinions · argument about greatness · futile thinking · evil thoughts from the heart · partiality: "judges with evil thoughts" · thoughts revealed by the child set for a sign | Luk 1:29 · Mar 8:16–17; Mat 16:7–8 · Mar 2:6, 8; Luk 5:21–22; 6:8; 9:47 · Luk 20:14; Mat 21:25 · Luk 12:17 · 1Ti 2:8 ("without anger or quarreling"); Phili 2:14; Rom 14:1 · Luk 9:46 · Rom 1:21; 1Co 3:20 · Mar 7:21; Mat 15:19 · Jam 2:4 · Luk 2:35 | Inner reasoning becomes outward quarrel when it is shared and set on one's own standing (Luk 9:46; Rom 14:1) (R). The heart state decides honest or hardened (Luk 1:29 against Mar 8:17, S). In 1Ti 2:8 the quarrel word stands beside anger, a link to the anger strand

What is held to be so is a state of the one who holds it: wise (1Cor 3:18, the wise within 2 words), religious (Jam 1:26), something when he is nothing (Gal 6:3), a prophet (1Cor 14:37), standing (1Cor 10:12), knowing (1Cor 8:2), with reason for confidence (Phili 3:4, confidence 6 before and 1 after) and thinking highly of oneself (Rom 12:3, faith 6 after). In each the object of the thinking is the thinker.

Fear stands within three words before the thought in Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, 2Sa 14:15 and Neh 6:9, in Luk 24:37 (startled and frightened, 3 and 1 words before) and in Gen 20:11 (the fear of God, 3 words after). In five of the six the fear is named before the thought and the thought comes from it.

Affliction, suffering and crying stand with the thought in Lam 1:9 (affliction), 1Cor 7:26 (the present distress, 3 words after), Phili 1:17 (afflict, 1 after), 1Pe 4:1 (Christ suffered, within 2 words), Luk 13:2 (suffered), Mar 6:49 (cried out, 4 after), Joh 11:31 and Joh 20:15 (weeping) and Deu 15:9 (the cry to the Lord, 14 after). The thinking is set in verses of distress or of a response to it.

Bearing follows the conceiving in six verses: 1 word after the member in Jdg 13:3, 13:5, 13:7 and Isa 7:14, 2 after in Mat 1:23 and 4 after in Luk 1:31; and calling the child's name follows in Isa 7:14 (3 after), Mat 1:23 (5) and Luk 1:31 (7). The conceiving is the first act of a pair or a series, bearing and naming.

Bearing meets the conceiving in six verses: 1 word after in Jdg 13:3, 13:5, 13:7 and Isa 7:14, 2 after in Mat 1:23 and 4 after in Luk 1:31. In every verse the bearing is the second act of the pair, conceive and bear; the verses are the bodily conceiving of a child and bear no inner-being meaning (researcher's ruling, #2527 v13).

The divine and the human are named in eight verses: God (4), the Lord and Jesus, with Immanuel (3), Sarah (2), the woman and the child. The messenger or the Lord announces the conceiving to the woman, the woman conceives and bears a son, and the child is called by the name the Lord gives; the direction of the announcement does not change across the verses.

Trust, loyalty and silence stand with the thought in 1Sa 27:12 (Achish trusted David, 2 words before), 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 (whom do you trust, 8 after), Mic 2:8 (trustingly, 1 before), Psa 48:9 and Psa 94:18 (steadfast love within 3 words) and Psa 50:21 (silence 1 word before the false supposition). Trust is the ground of Achish's thought, and the Lord's silence is the ground of the supposition that he is like the one who has done these things.

Asking and calling stand with the supposition in Mat 6:7 (those who pray suppose they will be heard), Mat 26:53 (the supposition whether Jesus cannot appeal), 2Sa 14:15 (the request the woman came to make), 2Ki 5:11 (Naaman supposes the prophet will call on the name of the Lord, 4 after), Jer 3:19 (call me Father, 1 after) and Jon 1:6 (call out to your god, 4 before the hope). The supposition is about being heard or about a call.

Evil and the wicked stand with the supposition in six verses. In Mat 9:4 'evil' is 1 word after the member and is what is thought; in 1Cor 14:20, Psa 64:5 and 1Ti 6:5 it or 'depraved' is 2 to 5 words before; in Pro 21:29 the wicked is 5 words before and is set against the upright who gives thought; in 2Sa 14:17 it is 14 after. The supposition is held by, or about, those described as evil.

Wisdom and understanding stand with the supposition in eight verses. The partner is within two words in Pro 14:15 (prudent, 1 before), Psa 73:16 (understand, 1 after), Ecc 9:10 (wisdom, 2 after) and 1Cor 3:18 (wise, 2 after), where the person thinks that he is wise; in 1Ch 28:9 (3 before), 2Sa 14:17 (12 after), Rom 2:3 (11 after) and 1Cor 7:40 (7 before) the partner is farther off.

Declaring meets the opinion and the thoughts in six verses. In Job 32:6, 32:10 and 32:17 'declare' is 2 words before the opinion and the opinion is what Elihu declares; in Psa 40:5 (proclaim, 4 after) and Isa 55:8 (declares, 4 after) the declaring follows the Lord's thoughts; in Dan 5:10 the queen declared 5 words before. The opinion is declared by the one who holds it and the thoughts are declared by the Lord.

Codes of the surfaces of this group have senses of their own that differ from 'thought': H8312 in Psa 139:23 (stored sense head 'anxiety'), H5587B in Job 20:2 (disquietings), H1902H in Lam 3:62 (the muttered musing of enemies), H1697I in Eze 38:10 (matters that come up), G0991 in Mat 22:16 and Mar 12:14 (a looking at persons, not an opinion held) and G3588 in 1Cor 2:11 (the article, morph empty, flagged in #2533). They are recorded as they stand in their verses.

Qualifiers of the thoughts are 'evil' directly before the noun in Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21 and Jam 2:4 (1 word before), 'wicked' in Jer 4:14 (1 before), 'very deep' in Psa 92:5 and 'of the righteous' and 'of the wicked' in Pro 12:5 and Pro 15:26. The adjective gives the thought its moral character in the verses of evil and its depth in the verse of the Lord's thoughts.

A supposition is held about another person or a state of affairs and acted on, and in the verses of the Gospels and Acts it proves mistaken or unverified: Mary supposed to be going to the tomb, the gardener, the group on the journey, Paul dead, the prisoners escaped, a ghost, a spirit, a sleep, a purchase, a vision. In each the verb of thinking states the supposition and the verse then states what the people did or found.

A person holds a view of himself, which the verse then tests: that he is wise (1Cor 3:18), something (Gal 6:3), religious (Jam 1:26), a prophet (1Cor 14:37), standing (1Cor 10:12), with grounds for confidence (Phili 3:4), and that he knows (1Cor 8:2). The verb states a self-estimate, and the verse sets it beside deceiving oneself, folly or knowledge.

What is held to be so is dying or perishing in Gen 26:9, Job 29:18 and Jon 1:6 (the dying stands 2 words after the member and is the content of the thought), escaping in Gen 32:8, Est 4:13, Act 16:27 and Rom 2:3 (the escape is within ten words and is part of what is supposed), and someone's being dead in 2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33 and Act 14:19.

The conceiving is stated of women whose condition the verse names: barren and not having borne (Jdg 13:3), clean and not defiled (Num 5:28), and in Heb 11:11 Sarah past the age; the negators of these verses reach the words defiled and borne, and in Jdg 13:5 and 13:7 they reach what the woman must not do (a razor, wine, unclean food). The conceiving is announced under a condition of the woman.

The poor and the rich stand with the supposition in five verses: 'poor' 10 words after in Deu 15:9, 'poor' 3 and 'needy' 2 before in Psa 40:17, 'rich' 4 before in Mic 2:8, 'poor' 17 after in Joh 13:29 and 'abundantly' 6 before in Eph 3:20. In Psa 40:17 and Deu 15:9 the poor are the ones the thought is directed to; in Joh 13:29 the disciples suppose a gift to the poor.

Honor and its opposite stand with the supposition in six verses: 'honoring' 4 words after in 2Sa 10:3 and 1Ch 19:3, 'worthy' 16 after in Act 13:25, 'honor' 9 before in Rom 1:21, 'less honorable' 1 and 'honor' 3 after in 1Cor 12:23, and disgrace 6 after in 1Ti 3:7. The supposition concerns what is honorable or reputed in the verses nearest the member.

Searching and finding stand with the supposition in ten verses. In Gen 18:28 and 18:30 'find' is the condition of each supposed number; in Joh 20:15 the seeking is 1 word before the supposition; in Joh 5:39 the search of the Scriptures is 4 words before; in Mat 18:12 (17 after), Luk 2:44 (9 after), 2Sa 10:3 and 1Ch 19:3 the search is in a later clause; in 1Ch 28:9 the Lord searches hearts 6 words before.

What is held to be so is peace and security in 2Ki 20:19 and Isa 39:8 (Hezekiah's thought, security 3 to 4 words after) and in Mat 10:34 and Luk 12:51 (the supposition that Jesus came to bring peace, which is corrected); and fortified cities in 2Ch 32:1 and a guard in Jer 40:5. The same word peace is held by Hezekiah and denied of Jesus' coming.

Fear and alarm meet the thoughts in six verses. In Dan 4:19, 5:6, 5:10 and 7:28 the thoughts are the subject of alarming, the alarm 1 to 2 words after; in Job 32:6 the speaker is afraid 4 words before declaring his opinion; in 2Cor 11:3 the fear (10 before) is Paul's fear about the readers' thoughts. The thoughts cause alarm in four and stand beside fear in two.

Wisdom and discernment meet the thoughts in six verses. In Psa 139:2 (discern, 1 before) and Heb 4:12 (discerning, 1 before) the thoughts are the object of discerning; in 1Cor 3:20 (wise, 1 after) the thoughts are of the wise and are futile; in Mic 4:12 (understand, 3 after), Pro 18:2 (understanding, 6 before) and Dan 2:30 (wisdom, 13 before) the partner is farther off.

Folly and the supposition meet in five verses: 'simple' 4 words before in Pro 14:15, 'foolish' 2 after in Rom 1:21, 'fool' 7 after in 1Cor 3:18, 'foolish' 2 and 'fool' 9 after in 2Cor 11:16 and 'fool' 8 before in 2Cor 12:6. Folly is what the thinking is judged to be, becomes, or is asked not to be taken for.

*raʿyôn* (Aramaic) | Night thoughts that carry revelation · thoughts that alarm | Dan 2:29–30 · Dan 4:19; 5:6, 10; 7:28 | The same night thoughts become revelation when God makes them known and an interpreter speaks (2:29–30; 5:10–12 points to Daniel). Without that they alarm, and the body shows it. Daniel's own alarm is kept, not acted on: "but I kept the matter in my heart" (7:28) (S)

Calling and the supposition meet in four verses. In 2Ki 5:11 (4 words after) and Jer 3:19 (1 after) the call is what the thinker expected would be made; in Jon 1:6 the command to call on his god stands 4 words before the hope that the god will give thought to them; in Gen 26:9 the calling of Isaac is 12 words before and is a separate act. The call is the expected or commanded act that the supposition concerns.

What is held to be so is another person's state or act: a prostitute (Gen 38:15, her face covered 2 words after), a gardener (Joh 20:15), in the group (Luk 2:44), drunk (Act 2:15), dead (Act 14:19), a sleep (Joh 11:13), a ghost (Mar 6:49), unclean (Rom 14:14, the uncleanness 2 words before) and not clean (1Sa 20:26). The object is a person or a thing in a state the speaker has not verified.

Commanding and the supposition meet in five verses. In Num 36:6 the Lord's commands stand 4 words before the thought of whom they think best; in 1Cor 14:37 the command (11 words after) is what the one who thinks he is a prophet is to acknowledge; in Psa 50:21 the charge (2 after) follows the false supposition about God; in Rom 12:3 and 2Sa 13:32 the partner is 8 and 12 words after, in later clauses. The supposition is set against a command or charge.

Sin stands with the supposition in five verses: 'sins' 5 words after in Eze 18:14, 'sinners' 5 after in Luk 13:2, 'sin' 6 after in 1Pe 4:1, 15 after in 1Cor 7:36 and 19 after in Deu 15:9. In Luk 13:2 and Eze 18:14 the sin is within the clause of what is supposed; in the other three it is in a later clause.

Life and death words stand with the supposition in eight verses. 'Dead' is 9, 4, 2 and 7 words after in 2Sa 13:32, 2Sa 13:33, Act 14:19 and Act 26:8, and in the first three the supposition is that someone is dead; 'alive' or 'lives' is 5 to 11 words after in 2Ki 7:12, 1Sa 20:3, 1Sa 27:11 and Luk 13:4. The state of being alive or dead is the commonest object of the supposition in this pairing.

Taking stands with the supposition in seven verses. In Luk 8:18 (taken, 2 after) and Act 8:20 (obtain, 1 after) the taking is what the supposed possession or what Simon supposed he could do; in 2Cor 10:5 'take' is 2 words before and acts on thought; in 2Sa 13:33, 2Ki 7:12, Mat 17:25 and Joh 20:15 it is a different act 4 to 17 words from the member.

Work stands with the supposition in four verses: 4 words after in Neh 6:9 (the work that will not be done), 1 before in Ecc 9:10 (no work or thought in Sheol), 11 after in Mat 21:28 and 3 after in Eph 3:20 (the power at work beyond what we think). Work is the thing the thought is about or set beside, not a tie of grammar.

Answering meets the thoughts and the opinion in five verses. In Job 20:2 and Luk 5:22 the answer is 1 word after the thoughts, as their occasion; in Dan 4:19 the king answers 3 words after; in Job 32:6 and Job 32:17 the answer stands 12 and 6 words before the opinion is declared. The thoughts are the occasion of an answer or are given in one.

Believing and the supposition meet in four verses with different ties. In Pro 14:15 the simple believes everything 3 words before the prudent gives thought, and the two are set against each other; in Rom 12:3, Phili 3:4 and Jam 1:26 the faith, confidence or religion is the thing the person thinks of himself, 1 to 12 words from the member. The supposition is about one's own standing in belief.

The thoughts are not known, not the same, not cared about: the nations do not know what the Lord thinks (Mic 4:12, the negator 2 words before the member), the Lord's thoughts are not our thoughts (Isa 55:8), and you do not care about anyone's opinion (Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14, the negator reaches 'care'). In each the thought or opinion is the object of a negated knowing, sameness or care.

H7476 *raʿyôn*. Only Daniel 7:28 is in the file. It is expected also in Daniel 2:29, 2:30, 4:19, 5:6 and 5:10. Daniel 2:29 matters for the question of origins: thoughts "came" to the king as he lay in bed.

A supposition issues in a spoken answer or a question in the exchanges of Gen 18:29 to 18:32, Gen 31:31, Exo 2:14, Est 4:13, Luk 7:43 and Luk 13:2: the supposition is put in the speaker's own words as part of a dialogue, with 'answered' 1 to 13 words from the member.

Answering and the supposition meet in nine verses: the four of Gen 18, where 'answered' is 4 words after each supposed number, Luk 7:43 (1 before), Luk 13:2 (2 before), Est 4:13 (3 before), Gen 31:31 (6 before) and Exo 2:14 (13 before). In every verse the supposition is said inside a spoken exchange of question and reply.

A gift or presence stands with the supposition in four verses with different senses. In Gen 32:20 the present (3 words after) is the means of appeasing, and in Jer 40:5 the present (7 after) is a gift; in Rut 4:4 ('presence') and 1Cor 7:26 ('present distress') the English word renders a place and a time, flagged in #2536. Only Gen 32:20 ties a gift to the supposition.

Intention meets the thoughts in four verses, of the same kind as the member: 'intention' 1 word before in Gen 6:5, 'purposes' 1 before in 1Ch 29:18, 'plan' 4 after in Mic 4:12 and 'intentions' 2 after in Heb 4:12. Thoughts and intentions are paired, as what a person holds or what the Lord holds and discerns.

Anger, hiding and hunger stand beside the thought in Gen 18:30 and Gen 18:32 (the Lord's anger), 2Ki 5:11 (Naaman's anger, 4 words before), Psa 64:5 (secretly, 1 word before), 2Ki 7:12 (hide, 2 words before; hungry, 6 before) and Gen 38:15 (the covering of her face, 2 words after). The thought arises in a person who is angry, hiding or hungry, or who is faced with something concealed.

Killing and the supposition meet in six verses: 1 word after in 2Sa 13:32 and 2Sa 21:16, 2 words before in Luk 13:4, Joh 16:2 and Act 16:27, and 4 to 5 before in Exo 2:14. In Joh 16:2 the killer supposes he serves God and in Act 16:27 the jailer supposes the prisoners have escaped; the killing is what is supposed or intended.

What is thought of is the steadfast love of the Lord in Psa 48:9 (1 word after the member), and what answers the thought of falling is the same steadfast love in Psa 94:18 (3 words after); the poor are the ones the Lord thinks of in Psa 40:17 (poor 3 before, needy 2 before) and the ones the unworthy thought turns from in Deu 15:9 (poor 10 after). The thinking is directed at the Lord's love or at the poor.

Reward and its opposite stand with the supposition in three verses: 'unworthy' 1 word before in Deu 15:9 (flagged in #2536 as stored under reward), 'pay' 2 after in Mat 22:17 and 'punishment' 1 before in Heb 10:29. In the two Gospel and Hebrew verses the thought asked of the hearer is about what is owed or what is deserved.

Trust stands with the supposition in four verses: 'trusted' 2 words before in 1Sa 27:12, 'trustingly' 1 before in Mic 2:8, and 'trust' 8 after in 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5. In 1Sa 27:12 Achish's trust is the ground of his thought, and in the two parallel verses the question whom they trust follows the supposed claim about words.

War and the supposition meet in four verses: in 2Ki 18:20 and Isa 36:5 war stands 5 words after the thought that words are strategy and power for it, in Mic 2:8 it is 1 word after the thought of the passersby, and in 1Sa 18:17 fight and battles stand 4 and 2 words before Saul's quoted thought. Conflict is what the supposed strength or the plan is for.

Silence and rest stand with the supposition in four verses: 'rest' 5 words after in 2Sa 14:17, 'silent' 1 before in Psa 50:21, 'remains' 3 before in 1Cor 7:40 and 'ceased' 5 after in 1Pe 4:1. Only in Psa 50:21 is the silence the ground of the supposition, that the one who is silent is like the one who accuses.

Security and the supposition meet in four verses: 'security' is 4 and 3 words after the thought of Hezekiah in 2Ki 20:19 and Isa 39:8, 'fortified' is 2 words before the thought of Sennacherib in 2Ch 32:1, and 'guard' is 4 after in Jer 40:5. In the first two security is the content of the thought; in the third the fortified cities are what he plans against.

Peace stands with the supposition in four verses: 2 to 4 words after in 2Ki 20:19, Isa 39:8, Mat 10:34 and Luk 12:51. The same word has two stances in the verses: Hezekiah supposes there will be peace in his days, and in Mat 10:34 and Luk 12:51 the supposition that Jesus came to bring peace is the one corrected.

Enduring and the supposition meet in four verses: 'withstand' is 1 word after the thought in 2Ch 13:8, 'remain' is 9 after in 1Cor 7:26 and 20 before in Jer 40:5, and 'last' is 6 after in 1Cor 4:9. In 2Ch 13:8 and 1Cor 7:26 the holding out or remaining is the content of the supposition or judgment.

An opinion is declared in Job 32:6, 32:10 and 32:17 (Elihu says he will declare his opinion, the declaring 2 words before) and laid bare in Pro 18:2 (the fool takes pleasure in expressing his heart). The opinion is a view held and then spoken, in the first three in an answer within a dialogue.

Face: Thinking and considering; Verses: Psa 73:16; 77:5; 119:59; Job 6:26; 35:2; Jer 23:27; Isa 29:16; What differs: Alone it is "a wearisome task" (Psa 73:16) "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (73:17). Turned on oneself it turns the feet (119:59). Turned on others' forgetting: "think to make my people forget my name by their dreams" (Jer 23:27); Why (basis): Where the thinking is done changes what it can see (S)

Truth, righteousness and the lawful stand with the supposition in Job 35:2 (just, 2 after), Mat 22:17 (lawful, 1 after), 2Cor 12:6 (truth, 5 before), 1Ti 6:5 (truth, 1 before), Phili 4:8 (honorable and just, 13 to 15 before) and Gen 18:28 (the righteous in the case put). The thought is a judgment whether something is right, true or lawful.

Righteousness, truth and the lawful stand with the supposition in six verses: 'just' 2 words after in Job 35:2, 'lawful' 1 after in Mat 22:17, 'truth' 5 before in 2Cor 12:6 and 1 before in 1Ti 6:5, 'honorable' and 'just' 15 and 13 before in Phili 4:8, and 'righteous' 3 after in Gen 18:28. In Job 35:2 and Mat 22:17 the supposition is the judgment whether something is just or lawful.

Wealth, teaching and counsel stand with the thought in a few verses: the imagination is the wall of the rich man's wealth (Pro 18:11, wealth 6 before), the thoughts are not to be cursed in even against the rich (Ecc 10:20, rich 7 after), the counsels of the wicked stand beside the thoughts of the righteous (Pro 12:5, 3 after), and the opinion of persons is set against teaching the way of God (Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14). The thought is set beside the wealth, the counsel or the teaching of the one who holds it.

Righteousness meets the thoughts in four verses: 'righteous' 1 and 'just' 2 words after in Pro 12:5, 'lawful' 8 after in Mar 12:14, and sexual immorality 3 and 1 words after in Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21, the next item in the list of what comes out of the heart. The thoughts of the righteous are set against the wicked's in Pro 12:5, and in the lists the evil thoughts head the sins.

Calling meets the conceiving in three verses, after the conceiving and the bearing: 'call' is 3 words after in Isa 7:14, 5 after in Mat 1:23 and 7 after in Luk 1:31, where the child's name is called. The calling of the name follows the conceiving of a son; the verses are the bodily conceiving of a child and bear no inner-being meaning (researcher's ruling, #2527 v13).

Thoughts come out of or arise in a person: evil thoughts come out of the heart in Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21 (the heart 3 to 4 words before, the thoughts the first of the things named), thoughts will come into the mind in Eze 38:10, and thoughts came to the king on his bed in Dan 2:29. The act is the arising of a thought in the heart or mind, and in the first two it issues in the acts that the verses list after it.

The thoughts alarm the one who has them in Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10 and Dan 7:28: the thoughts are the subject of the alarming, the verb stands 1 to 2 words after the member, and the change of color is named within five words. The act runs from the thoughts to the person.

*enthymēsis / dianoēma* | Thoughts known by Jesus · thoughts and intentions discerned by the word · imagination that makes images of God | Mat 9:4; 12:25; Luk 11:17 · Heb 4:12 · Act 17:29 | "an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Act 17:29). Imagination is the faculty of design (*ḥāšav* G) turned to making gods. This is the Greek counterpart of Hab 2:18 and the false likening of *dāmāh* (S/R)

Blessing words stand far from the supposition in three verses: grace 11 words before in Rom 12:3, a willing gift 16 words after in 2Cor 9:5 and grace 16 after in Heb 10:29. At these distances the partner is in another clause, and the two work together only in that the same verse speaks of what is given and of what is thought of oneself or others; no tie of grammar joins them.

The outward act that follows a supposition is stated in the same verse: the Jews follow Mary (Joh 11:31, going 2 words after), Joseph's people go a day's journey (Luk 2:44), the crowds stone Paul (Act 14:19), the jailer draws his sword (Act 16:27, killing 2 words before), the sailors weigh anchor (Act 27:13), Saul gives his daughter as a snare (1Sa 18:21, give 1 after), and Jacob sends a present (Gen 32:20, present 3 after). The supposition and the act it leads to stand in the one sentence.

The intention of the heart: "every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Gen 6:5); "the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Gen 8:21) — said by the Lord "in his heart"; "keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you" (1Ch 29:18); "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1Ch 28:9); "disclose the purposes of the heart" (1Co 4:5)

Concealing and the supposition meet in three verses: the covering of her face (2 words after) is the ground of Judah's supposition in Gen 38:15; hiding (2 before) and secretly (1 before) stand beside the quoted thoughts of the Syrians and of the wicked in 2Ki 7:12 and Psa 64:5. The thought is formed from, or alongside, something concealed.

Crying and weeping stand with the supposition in four verses: 'cry' 14 words after in Deu 15:9, 'cried out' 4 after in Mar 6:49, weeping 6 after in Joh 11:31 and weeping before in Joh 20:15. In the three Gospel verses the crying or weeping follows or accompanies a supposition about a ghost, the tomb or the gardener.

Departing and the supposition meet in four verses. In Joh 11:31 the going out is 2 words after the supposition that explains it; in 1Sa 27:11 'leave' is 5 words before the quoted thought of David; in Ecc 9:10 and Mat 18:12 the going or leaving is 7 and 12 words from the member in other clauses. Only in Joh 11:31 is the departure the act that the supposition leads to.

Cleanness and uncleanness stand with the supposition in three verses: 'unclean' 2 words before and after and 7 before in Rom 14:14, 'clean' 4 and 7 after in 1Sa 20:26 and 'uncleanness' 5 before in Lam 1:9. In Rom 14:14 the uncleanness is the object of the thinking and depends on it; in 1Sa 20:26 Saul's thought is that David is not clean.

Asking stands with the supposition in three verses: 'pray' 6 words before in Mat 6:7, 'appeal' 3 after in Mat 26:53 and 'request' 7 after in 2Sa 14:15. In Mat 6:7 those who pray suppose they will be heard for many words; in Mat 26:53 the supposition is whether Jesus cannot appeal to the Father.

Pain and hunger stand with the supposition in three verses: 'hungry' 6 words before in 2Ki 7:12, 'suffered' 10 after in Luk 13:2, and 'suffered' 5 before and 2 after in 1Pe 4:1. In 1Pe 4:1 the suffering of Christ is within two words of the way of thinking the readers are to arm themselves with.

Loyalty and steadfast love stand with the supposition in three verses: steadfast love is 1 word after the thought in Psa 48:9 and 3 after in Psa 94:18, and faithfulness is 10 before in 2Ch 32:1. In Psa 48:9 the Lord's love is what is thought on, and in Psa 94:18 it answers the thought that the foot slips.

The figurative conceiving of what is then borne is a done act in Job 15:35 (trouble conceived and evil borne), Isa 33:11 (chaff conceived and stubble borne) and Isa 59:4 (mischief conceived and iniquity borne). The same code H2029 whose Poel sense is to contrive or devise is used of bodily conceiving in Jdg 13:3; in these three verses what is conceived is evil and what is borne is evil or stubble.

Conceiving is a done act in Psa 51:5 (the speaker's mother conceived him) and in Heb 11:11 (Sarah received power to conceive); in the Greek verse the conceiving is carried by a phrase of two nouns, 'laying down' and 'seed', and in Mat 1:23 by the verb 'to have' with 'in'. The act is bodily and is stated of a woman in each verse.

Teaching meets the thoughts and the opinion in three verses: 'counsels' 3 words after in Pro 12:5, and 'teach' 9 before in Mat 22:16 and 5 after in Mar 12:14, where the opinion of persons is set against teaching the way of God. The counsels of the wicked are paired with the thoughts of the righteous, and the Teacher is said not to regard opinion.

Where the thoughts of persons are given up, set against God's or left uncared for, the act is a refusal as the verses state it: the unrighteous man is to forsake his thoughts (Isa 55:7) and the opinion of persons is not regarded (Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14). Where the psalmist asks to be known the act is a pursuit.

Returning stands with the supposition in three verses: 5 words after in Jer 3:7 (expected and not done), 8 after in Heb 11:15 (what thinking of the land would have allowed) and 19 before in Jer 40:5. In Jer 3:7 and Heb 11:15 the return is what the thought leads toward and in Jer 3:7 it does not happen.

Affliction stands with the supposition in three verses: 'afflict' 1 word after in Phili 1:17, 'distress' 3 after in 1Cor 7:26 and 'affliction' 8 after in Lam 1:9. In Phili 1:17 the thought is of afflicting Paul and the affliction is 1 word after it; in 1Cor 7:26 the distress is the ground of the judgment.

A change of color meets the thoughts in three Aramaic verses: 'changed' is 1 word before in Dan 5:6, 'change' 3 after in Dan 5:10 and 'changed' 5 after in Dan 7:28. In each verse the thoughts alarm the person and the bodily change is named within five words, so the thoughts and the visible effect are stated together.

Words of life meet the thoughts in three verses: 'living' 9 words before in Dan 2:30, 'live' 3 before in Dan 5:10 (live forever) and 'living' 19 before in Heb 4:12 (the word is living). The distances and the phrases show no tie of grammar between the living and the thoughts.

Deceiving and the supposition meet in three verses: 6 words before in 1Cor 3:18, 5 after in Gal 6:3 and 8 after in Jam 1:26. In all three the person thinks something of himself and the verse names self-deception beside it, so the supposition about oneself and the deceit of oneself are stated together.

Where the supposition is held and acted on the act is a pursuit of its content: the people follow Mary out, go a day's journey, stone Paul, draw the sword, sail on, send a gift, give a daughter to a snare. The thought is the ground of a move toward the thing supposed.

Escaping and the supposition meet in four verses: 9 words after in Gen 32:8, 4 after in Est 4:13, 2 after in Act 16:27 and 10 after in Rom 2:3. In every verse the escape is part of what is supposed: hoped for by Jacob, denied to Esther, assumed by the jailer and put to the judge as a question.
yēṣer ("intention", "inclination") is the same word as the potter's thing formed, and as our frame.

Judging and the supposition meet in four verses. In Joh 5:45 (accuse, 3 after) and Rom 2:3 (judge, 3 after) the supposition concerns accusation or judgment; in Luk 7:43 the judging (8 after) is the answer given to Simon's supposition; in Exo 2:14 'judge' is 8 words before, in the question the accuser puts to Moses. The supposition and the judging are set side by side in each.

Comfort and the supposition meet in three verses with different relations. In Psa 119:52 the thinking of the Lord's rules and the comfort taken are in one clause, comfort 4 words after; in Job 12:5 the at-ease (1 word after the thought) hold contempt for misfortune; in Joh 11:31 the consoling stands 10 words before the supposition that explains why they followed Mary out.

A thought is asked to be searched and known in Psa 139:23 (search me and know my thoughts, the knowing 2 words before) and a person is told to forsake his thoughts in Isa 55:7 (the unrighteous man his thoughts, 5 words after the wicked). The first is asked of God and the second is said by the Lord of a person.
Where the psalmist asks that his thoughts be known and tried (Psa 139:23) and speaks of the Lord's thoughts as precious (Psa 139:17) the act is a pursuit of what is asked or valued.

Works meet the thoughts in three verses: the works are 3 words before in Psa 92:5 and 1 before in Isa 66:18, where God's works and God's thoughts, or the works and thoughts of the nations, are paired, and 10 before in Rom 2:15 where the law's work is set in the hearts. In the first two the pairing is of the Lord's works with his thoughts.

Wealth meets the thoughts in three verses: 'wealth' 6 words before the imagination in Pro 18:11 (the wall of the rich man's wealth), 'rich' 7 after in Ecc 10:20 (not to curse the rich even in your thoughts) and 'abundantly' 8 after in Isa 55:7. Only in Pro 18:11 is wealth the thing the imagination pictures.

Destroying and the supposition meet in five verses. In Gen 18:28, 18:31 and 18:32 the destroying is what the Lord is asked not to do under each supposed number; in Isa 10:7 it is 3 words after the thought and is the purpose in the heart that is said not to be what he thinks; in 2Cor 10:5 it is 12 words before and is an act on arguments. The supposition is the case on which the destroying is argued or the plan that destroying belongs to.

Searching and finding stand with the supposition in Gen 18:28 and Gen 18:30 ('find' is the condition of each supposed number), Mat 18:12, Luk 2:44 and Joh 20:15 (the search follows the supposition or the question) and Joh 5:39 (searching the Scriptures, 4 words before the supposition). The supposition is set in a verse of a search or of a condition to be found.

The evil thoughts come out of the heart together with the acts the verses list after them: sexual immorality 1 to 3 words after the member in Mat 15:19 and Mar 7:21, with murder, adultery, theft, false witness and slander in the same list. The thought is the first of the things that come out and the acts follow it in the same sentence.

Persuading and the supposition meet in three verses: persuaded stands 8 words before the supposition of the crowds in Act 14:19 and 13 before Paul's thought of the unclean in Rom 14:14, and obeying stands 3 words after the thought taken captive in 2Cor 10:5. The persuasion is a separate earlier act in the first two, and the obedience is the end of the thought in the third.

The English word "thought" picks up rows that aren't about the inner life. 1 Timothy 3:7 ("well thought of"), Acts 15:38, 2 Corinthians 9:5 and Philippians 2:25.
5. Suggested exclusions. Idiomatic uses such as "well thought of" (1 Tim 3:7) and "thought it necessary" (2 Cor 9:5, Phil 2:25).

In Num 11:12 the conceiving is put as a rhetorical question: Moses asks whether he conceived all this people and gave them birth. The question presupposes that he did not, so the conceiving is stated as not done by him and the bodily word is used of his relation to the people.
In Num 11:12 the act is a refusal as the question puts it: Moses denies having conceived the people and so denies the charge laid on him.

Anger and the supposition meet in three verses. In Gen 18:30 and Gen 18:32 the Lord's anger is what Abraham asks not to be roused, 2 and 4 words before the supposed number, and the supposition is the case he puts while the anger is held back; in 2Ki 5:11 Naaman's own anger stands 4 words before his quoted thought. The anger is the setting of the supposition, the Lord's in the first two and the thinker's in the third.

Small words stand in the units of the surfaces of this group and do not carry the sense of conceiving or devising: the preposition H5921A in Psa 41:7, the Greek 'in' (G1722) in Mat 1:23 and the verb 'to have' (G2192) read with it, which together form the idiom rendered conceive. They are read in their verses as standalone beside the member that gives the sense; the grouping placed the whole surface 'conceive' under devising although most of its occurrences are bodily conceiving, which was left as uncertain.

One word covers both inner reasoning and outward dispute. *Dialogismos* is rendered "thoughts" (Mark 7:21), but also "quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8), "disputing" (Philippians 2:14) and "opinions" (Romans 14:1). The same activity happens inside a person as an inner conversation and between people as argument.
Reasoning within one heart and reasoning between people are one word (dialogizomai)

to_trace.text: The Greek is the idiom of having in the womb: the woman will be with child. It is bodily conception, said of the virgin in the quoted prophecy. Verses: Mat 1:23.

The Greek noun is the laying down of seed; with the next word it makes the phrase the English renders as the power to conceive, said of Sarah past the age. It names the act of conceiving, not a thought. Verses: Heb 11:11.
The Greek noun is seed, the word that completes the phrase rendered the power to conceive in this verse; the English folds the pair into one verb. Verses: Heb 11:11.
The Greek verb is to take together and so to conceive in the womb; the angel tells Mary she will conceive and bear a son. It is bodily conception. Verses: Luk 1:31.
In these two verses the Hebrew verb is bodily conception: Moses asks whether he conceived the people, and the angel tells the barren woman she will conceive. Verses: Num 11:12, Judg 13:3.

In these three verses the same verb is used figuratively: wicked people conceive trouble, chaff and mischief and give birth to evil, iniquity and stubble. The picture of pregnancy carries what is formed in a person and then brought out in act. Verses: Job 15:35, Isa 33:11, Isa 59:4.
The Hebrew verb is bodily conception, the angel's announcement of a son and the sign of the virgin; it is a promise of birth, not a thought. Verses: Judg 13:5, Judg 13:7, Isa 7:14.
The Hebrew verb is to be sown with seed: the woman cleared of defilement will be able to conceive children. It is bodily conception. Verses: Num 5:28.
The Hebrew verb is the warming that conceives: the psalmist says his mother conceived him in sin. It is bodily conception, with sin placed at its start. Verses: Psa 51:5.

In these two verses the Greek is a verb of looking; the phrase is that Jesus does not look at the face of men, which the English renders as caring for no one's opinion. It names regard for other people's standing, not a view of his own. Verses: Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14.
In Job 32 'opinion' is Elihu's own view or knowledge, which he is afraid at first to declare because of his youth and then insists on declaring. Verses: Job 32:6, Job 32:10, Job 32:17.
In Pro 18:2 the Hebrew is the word for heart, the fool's own mind: he takes pleasure only in revealing what his heart holds, which the English renders as his opinion. Verses: Pro 18:2.
In Rom 1:21 'thinking' is the reasonings of the mind, the plural inner deliberation that became futile when people knew God and did not honor him. Verses: Rom 1:21.
In 2Cor 12:19 'thinking' is the readers assuming something, that Paul has been defending himself to them; the verse corrects it. Verses: 2Cor 12:19.
In 1Pe 4:1 'way of thinking' is the intent or mind-set believers are to arm themselves with, set beside Christ's suffering. Verses: 1Pe 4:1.
In Rom 1:21 this code is the Greek conjunction in the clause about becoming futile in thinking; it joins clauses and carries no thinking, which G1261 carries. Verses: Rom 1:21.
In Heb 11:15 'thinking of' is keeping in mind or remembering the land they left; the verse says that if they had kept it in mind they could have returned. Verses: Heb 11:15.
In Phili 1:17 'thinking' is supposing or intending: some preach out of ambition, expecting to add affliction to Paul in prison. Verses: Phili 1:17.
In 1Cor 14:20 'thinking' is the mind or understanding, the Greek noun for the seat of understanding; believers are not to be children in it, but mature. Verses: 1Cor 14:20.

In these eight verses the Hebrew verb of saying introduces a thought quoted as a sentence: Jacob, David, Achish, the Jebusites, the king of Israel, Sennacherib, Nehemiah's enemies and the wicked each 'say' it in themselves. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will not be seen. Verses: Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9, Psa 64:5.

In these seven verses 'thinks' is holding an estimate of oneself, that one has something, is wise, stands, is a prophet, is something, has confidence in the flesh, or is religious. Each time the verse tests the estimate and finds it wanting or sets another beside it. Verses: Luk 8:18, 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4, Jam 1:26.
In Rom 14:14 'thinks it unclean' is the reckoning of the person: the thing is unclean for the one who counts it so, though nothing is unclean in itself. Verses: Rom 14:14.
In 1Cor 7:36 'thinks' is judging his own conduct toward his betrothed to be improper; the Greek is a verb of holding as so, and the judgment is the man's own. Verses: 1Cor 7:36.
In 1Sa 20:3 'thinks' is the Hebrew verb of saying, quoting what Saul says in himself: that Jonathan must not know. It is inner speech about another person. Verses: 1Sa 20:3.
In 2Pe 1:13 this code is the Greek conjunction in the clause 'I think it right'; it carries no thinking, which the verb of G2233 carries. Verses: 2Pe 1:13.

In these seven verses 'think' is a question put to a hearer for his view: 'What do you think?' asks Jesus, and the hearers are asked about a case, a person or a coming. It asks for a judgment the hearer already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.

In these verses 'think' is holding a belief, often one the verse then corrects: the Gentiles' belief that many words are heard, the belief that Jesus cannot appeal to his Father, that he came to give peace, that the Galileans were worse, that the Scriptures give life apart from him, that killing believers serves God. In the Pauline verses it is Paul's own estimate of the apostles' place, of his judgment, of the body's parts and of the foolish. Verses: Mat 6:7, Mat 26:53, Luk 12:51, Luk 13:2, Luk 13:4, Joh 5:39, Joh 5:45, Joh 16:2, 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23, 2Cor 11:16, Heb 10:29.
In Mat 9:4 'think evil' is to turn something over in the mind: Jesus asks why they entertain evil in their hearts, and the verse names the heart as the place. Verses: Mat 9:4.
In 2Pe 1:13 'I think it right' is judging or counting it fitting: Peter counts it right to remind them while he lives. Verses: 2Pe 1:13.
In 2Cor 12:6 'think more of me' is the estimate others form: Paul holds back lest anyone credit him with more than they see or hear. Verses: 2Cor 12:6.
In Phili 4:8 'think about these things' is a command to direct the mind to what is true, honorable and excellent: to reckon with them and dwell on them. Verses: Phili 4:8.
In Eph 3:20 'think' is to take in with the mind, to conceive: God does more than all that we ask or conceive, set beside asking. Verses: Eph 3:20.

In these verses 'think' is to hold something as so: Jesus tells the hearers not to suppose he came to abolish the law or bring peace, Paul says God is not to be thought like an image, and Paul gives his own judgment on remaining as one is. In the first three the held notion is a wrong one the verse corrects; in 1Cor 7:26 it is a considered view. Verses: Mat 5:17, Mat 10:34, Act 17:29, 1Cor 7:26.

In Rom 12:3 and Phili 3:15 'think' is the mind-set, the way one is minded: not to rate oneself above what is right but to be sober, and to hold the same mind or another. The verb names the direction of the mind, with a measure given. Verses: Rom 12:3, Phili 3:15.

In these four verses the Hebrew verb of saying is rendered 'think': the Assyrian asks whether words are strategy, the Chronicler accuses Israel of thinking to withstand the Lord, and the Spirit says so the house of Israel thinks. It is the inner or said claim of those addressed. Verses: 2Ki 18:20, 2Ch 13:8, Isa 36:5, Eze 11:5.
In Est 4:13 'think' is the Hebrew verb of imagining or supposing: Mordecai warns Esther not to imagine to herself that she alone will escape. Verses: Est 4:13.
In Psa 119:52 'think of' is to call to mind: the psalmist recalls the Lord's rules from of old and takes comfort. Verses: Psa 119:52.

In Isa 10:7 'think' is the Hebrew verb of planning and devising: the Assyrian's heart is not set on the plan the Lord has, for his own purpose is destruction of nations; the verb is of planning. Verses: Isa 10:7.

In these three verses 'think' is reckoning or counting: whether one holds a thing just, whether one would reckon the deep to be white-haired, and what God counts the son of man to be. Verses: Job 35:2, Job 41:32, Psa 144:3.
In Job 6:26 and Jer 23:27 'think' is to plan or intend: Job asks whether his friends intend to reprove words, and the prophets intend to make the people forget the name. Verses: Job 6:26, Jer 23:27.
In Psa 119:59 'think' is to reflect: the psalmist considers his ways and turns his feet to the testimonies; the reflection leads to action. Verses: Psa 119:59.
In Dan 7:25 'think' is the Aramaic verb of intending: the one who speaks against the Most High means to change the times and the law. Verses: Dan 7:25.

In these four verses 'think' renders the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom 'in the eyes of': what seems right or best to someone. It is how a person sees or judges a matter. Verses: Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:5.
In 2Sa 18:27 'I think' is the watchman's judgment from what he sees: the running of the first is like that of Ahimaaz. It is an impression from sight. Verses: 2Sa 18:27.

In these seven verses 'thoughts' are the reasonings of the mind, which come out of the heart, are known or perceived by Jesus, are revealed from many hearts, are futile for the wise, and become evil in the judge. They are inner reasonings with the heart as their place and Jesus as their knower. Verses: Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, 1Cor 3:20, Jam 2:4.
In Luk 11:17 'thoughts' is the inner thinking of the hearers that Jesus knows before he answers. Verses: Luk 11:17.
In Luk 1:51 'thoughts' is the mind or understanding of the proud, scattered by the Lord's arm. Verses: Luk 1:51.

In Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25 and Heb 4:12 'thoughts' is inner reflection that Jesus knows and that the word of God discerns; the two Matthew verses have Jesus answer them, and Hebrews names them with the intentions of the heart. Verses: Mat 9:4, Mat 12:25, Heb 4:12.
In 2Cor 11:3 'thoughts' are the mind's products or schemes, which Paul fears will be led astray from devotion to Christ as Eve was. Verses: 2Cor 11:3.

In 1Cor 2:11 this code is the Greek article in 'the things of a person', which the English renders as a person's thoughts; the verse says only the person's spirit knows them, as only God's Spirit knows God's. Verses: 1Cor 2:11.

In Eze 38:10 'thoughts' is the Hebrew word for words or matters that come up, here the matters that rise in the mind of Gog before he devises a scheme: something arises, then the person works on it. Verses: Eze 38:10.
In Lam 3:62 'thoughts' is the murmuring of the assailants, the Hebrew word for what is muttered or devised, set with their lips against the speaker all day. Verses: Lam 3:62.
In Ecc 10:20 'thoughts' is the mind or knowledge within, where a person might curse the king; the verse warns that even there it may be carried. Verses: Ecc 10:20.
In Psa 10:4 'thoughts' are the wicked man's schemes or devices, summed up as that there is no God. Verses: Psa 10:4.

In these verses 'thoughts' are the purposes and devisings of people: the intention of the heart in Gen 6:5, purposes kept in the heart in 1Ch 29:18, schemes against others, the just thoughts of the righteous and the foul ones of the wicked, the thoughts to be forsaken, thoughts of iniquity, the thoughts God knows and wicked thoughts that lodge within. Verses: Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Job 21:27, Psa 56:5, Psa 94:11, Pro 12:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7, Isa 66:18, Jer 4:14.
In Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5 and Mic 4:12 'thoughts' are the Lord's: his thoughts toward his people, very deep, and a plan that the nations do not know. Verses: Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Mic 4:12.
In Isa 55:8 and Isa 55:9 the same word sets God's thoughts against man's: his are not ours and are as high above ours as heaven is above the earth. Verses: Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9.
In Job 20:2 'thoughts' are the disquieting thoughts that press on Zophar and answer him from within, because of his haste. Verses: Job 20:2.
In Psa 139:2 and Psa 139:17 'thoughts' are what the mind holds: the psalmist's thought is known to God from afar, and God's thoughts are precious and vast to him. Verses: Psa 139:2, Psa 139:17.

In these Aramaic verses 'thoughts' are the thoughts that rise in the mind: in Dan 2:29 thoughts come in bed about what will be, and in the other verses the king's and Daniel's thoughts alarm them. The same thoughts carry revelation in one place and fear in the others. Verses: Dan 2:29, Dan 2:30, Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10, Dan 7:28.
In Psa 139:23 'thoughts' are the anxious thoughts that the psalmist asks God to search and know, with the heart named beside them. Verses: Psa 139:23.
In Luk 12:17 'thought' is reasoning within oneself: the rich man deliberates in himself what to do about his crops. Verses: Luk 12:17.

In these five verses 'thought' is supposing something to be so: the disciples take Jesus for a ghost, the others take him for a spirit, the disciples take his word of sleep as rest, some take Judas's errand as a purchase, and Peter takes the angel's act for a vision. In each case the supposition is wrong. Verses: Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29, Act 12:9.
In 2Cor 9:5 and Phili 2:25 'thought it necessary' is judging or counting it needful: Paul decides on the sending he describes. Verses: 2Cor 9:5, Phili 2:25.
In Act 26:8 'thought' is judged: Paul asks why it is judged incredible by the hearers that God raises the dead. Verses: Act 26:8.
In Luk 12:17 the Greek is the verb of saying; the English 'he thought to himself' renders it as what the man said in himself. It is inner speech. Verses: Luk 12:17.

In 1Ti 3:7 'well thought of' is the Greek noun for testimony or good report: the overseer is to have a good report from those outside. It is how others speak of him, not what he thinks. Verses: 1Ti 3:7.
In 2Cor 10:5 'thought' is the mind's product: Paul takes every thought captive to obey Christ, set beside arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. Verses: 2Cor 10:5.

In Mat 20:10 and Act 8:20 'thought' is an assumption of the person: the workers hired first expect more, and Simon assumes the gift of God can be bought. In both the verse shows the assumption to be wrong. Verses: Mat 20:10, Act 8:20.
In 1Cor 13:11 'thought' is how the child was minded; the verse sets it with speaking and reasoning as childish ways given up in adulthood. Verses: 1Cor 13:11.
In Jon 1:6 this code is the Hebrew particle 'perhaps' in the captain's hope that the god may give a thought to them; it carries a possibility, with no thinking of its own. Verses: Jon 1:6.

In these twenty-five verses 'thought' is the Hebrew verb of saying, quoting what a person says in himself: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, the servants, Saul, David's woman of Tekoa, Naaman, Hezekiah, the psalmist and others each state in a quoted sentence what they judged or expected, and the verse usually shows the thought wrong or about to be tested. It is inner speech about what will happen or what others mean. Verses: Gen 20:11, Gen 26:9, Gen 31:31, Gen 32:20, Exo 2:14, Jos 22:28, Judg 3:24, Judg 15:2, Rut 4:4, 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 18:11, 1Sa 18:17, 1Sa 18:21, 1Sa 20:26, 2Sa 14:15, 2Sa 14:17, 2Sa 21:16, 2Ki 5:11, 2Ki 20:19, Job 29:18, Psa 94:18, Isa 39:8, Jer 3:7, Jer 3:19, Eze 20:32.

In Pro 14:15 and Pro 21:29 'gives thought to his steps' is attending carefully to one's way: the prudent and the upright consider where they go, set against the simple and the wicked. Verses: Pro 14:15, Pro 21:29.
In Deu 15:9 'thought' is the Hebrew word for a matter or word that arises in the heart, here an unworthy one against lending near the year of release. Verses: Deu 15:9.
In Num 33:56 'thought to do' is the Lord's own intention toward the Israelites if they fail to drive the people out: what he planned for others, he will do to them. Verses: Num 33:56.
In Psa 48:9 'thought on' is meditating on the Lord's steadfast love in the temple; the Hebrew is to dwell on something with the mind. Verses: Psa 48:9.
In Psa 50:21 'thought' is the false likeness the wicked imagine: that God is one like themselves. The Hebrew is of likening, and it is rebuked. Verses: Psa 50:21.
In Deu 15:9 this code is the Hebrew verb 'to be' in the clause 'lest there be an unworthy thought'; it carries no thinking, which the noun of H1697 carries. Verses: Deu 15:9.
In Lam 1:9 'took no thought' is the Hebrew verb of remembering: Jerusalem did not remember or consider her end. Verses: Lam 1:9.

In 1Sa 18:25 and Psa 40:17 'thought' is the Hebrew verb of devising and taking thought: Saul plans an end for David, and the Lord takes thought for the poor psalmist. In the first it is a plan against a person; in the second care for one. Verses: 1Sa 18:25, Psa 40:17.
In Gen 38:15 'thought' is reckoning or taking someone for something: Judah takes the veiled woman for a prostitute. Verses: Gen 38:15.
In Psa 73:16 'thought' is to reflect and try to understand: the psalmist turns the matter over and finds it wearisome until he enters the sanctuary. Verses: Psa 73:16.
In Ecc 9:10 'thought' is the Hebrew noun for reckoning or account: the verse says there is no work, reckoning, knowledge or wisdom in Sheol. Verses: Ecc 9:10.
In 1Ch 28:9 'thought' is the Hebrew word for a plan or device that the Lord understands, with every heart searched; David tells Solomon to serve with a whole heart. Verses: 1Ch 28:9.
In 2Sa 3:19 'thought good' renders the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom 'in the eyes of': what seemed good to Israel and Benjamin. Verses: 2Sa 3:19.
In Jon 1:6 'give a thought' is the Hebrew verb of taking thought or caring: the captain hopes the god will think of them so they may not perish. Verses: Jon 1:6.
In Job 12:5 'thought' is the Hebrew noun for the settled thinking of the one at ease: it despises misfortune. The verse ties the thought to the circumstance of ease. Verses: Job 12:5.
In Mic 2:8 'with no thought of war' is the Hebrew verb of turning back from war: the trusting passers-by who are stripped have returned from fighting. Verses: Mic 2:8.
In Amo 4:13 'thought' is the Hebrew word for musing or meditation: God declares to man what his own thought is, as the maker of mountains and wind. Verses: Amo 4:13.

senses.obs_text: God's thoughts, and the contrast with man's: his thoughts toward his people are many and very deep, the nations do not know the Lord's thoughts, his thoughts are not man's and are as high above them as the heavens, and his thoughts are precious to the psalmist. The thoughts are the Lord's own purposes and mind. Verses: Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Psa 139:17, Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9, Mic 4:12.

Conceiving evil as if in a womb: wicked people conceive trouble, chaff and mischief and give birth to evil, stubble and iniquity. The same verb of conceiving is turned to what a person forms within and brings out in act. Verses: Job 15:35, Isa 33:11, Isa 59:4.

Conceiving a child: the woman becomes pregnant and bears, in the promises and announcements of a son, in the question of the barren, in the cleansed woman who will conceive, in the confession of the psalmist that his mother conceived him in sin, and in the sign of the virgin. The words are Hebrew and Greek verbs and nouns of pregnancy and seed, and the English 'conceive' is bodily. Verses: Num 5:28, Num 11:12, Judg 13:3, Judg 13:5, Judg 13:7, Psa 51:5, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23, Luk 1:31, Heb 11:11.

'Opinion' in the phrase about not caring for anyone's opinion: the Greek verb is of looking, and the phrase is that Jesus does not look at the person's face, that is, does not weigh people by standing. It is regard for status, not a view held. Verses: Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14.

Opinion as a view that a person holds and declares: Elihu is afraid to declare his opinion and then insists on it, and the fool takes pleasure only in declaring what his heart holds. It is a person's own view, set against understanding. Verses: Job 32:6, Job 32:10, Job 32:17, Pro 18:2.
'Perhaps' as the captain's hope that the god may give a thought to them: the Hebrew particle of possibility, carrying no thinking of its own. Verses: Jon 1:6.
'With no thought of war' as turning back from war: the Hebrew verb is of returning, said of the trusting passers-by who are stripped. It is a turning back, not a thought. Verses: Mic 2:8.
'Well thought of' as a good report: the Greek noun is of testimony, the overseer must have a good report from outsiders. It is how others speak of him, not what he thinks. Verses: 1Ti 3:7.

Thinking as the way the mind works, its understanding or frame: the thinking of people who knew God becomes futile, the believers are to be mature and not children in their thinking, and they are to arm themselves with Christ's way of thinking. It is the mind's mode, with a measure of maturity or futility. Verses: Rom 1:21, 1Cor 14:20, 1Pe 4:1.

A question that asks for a hearer's view: 'what do you think?' is put to Simon, to the hearers, to the lawyer, to the chief priests and to those looking for Jesus. It asks the person to give a judgment he already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.

What seems right or best in someone's eyes: the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom of what appears good to a person, rendered think, think best or thought good. It is a person's own judgment of what is good or fitting. Verses: Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:4, Jer 40:5, 2Sa 3:19.

A thought quoted as inner speech: the Hebrew verb of saying introduces what a person says in himself, and the quoted sentence gives the thought; the Greek of Luk 12:17 does the same with the rich man's words to himself. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will follow, and the verse often shows it wrong. The word is attention of the mind to a matter or person.
